analysis.reflection: There is no codebase, which is correct for this role — judged in operations terms, the JD is rich enough to ground a confident read. The real 'body of work' is a residential-homebuilding purchasing operation: a PO/WO system, a vendor/subcontractor database, house files, outside takeoffs/estimates, vendor invoices, and the CBUSA buying cooperative, run mostly on Microsoft Office. The headline divergence is the label: this is a residential-construction Purchasing Agent/Buyer mis-titled as a generic 'Supply Chain Analyst.' The actual work is competitive sourcing, qualifying trade subcontractors, generating POs/WOs, pricing options and change orders, and standing up purchasing processes — relationship- and administration-driven, not the demand-planning/inventory-analytics work the title implies. 'Must have construction experience, preferably residential' is a hard gate the title hides, and the scope (own the system, write the manual, present to the management committee) reads heavier than the stated 'medior' level — closer to a purchasing lead/manager. Anyone sourced against the title rather than the task list will be the wrong candidate.

case.title: Purchasing Agent Work-Sample: Level a trade-bid package, price a change order, and reconcile invoices for one spec home
case.brief: You are stepping into the senior Purchasing Agent seat at a residential homebuilder. The provided starting materials are a real fit for this role, so you will work them the way a Purchasing Agent actually does: sourcing and leveling subcontractor pricing, pricing options/change orders against scopes and takeoffs, reconciling vendor invoices, and advancing the PO/WO system toward paperless. You are NOT being tested on typing or on producing volume — assume any spreadsheet, memo, or rule you write could be machine-drafted in seconds. What we are evaluating is your judgment: how you normalize messy bids, what you confirm before committing a number to a sub or a price to Sales, what you read before you dispute a vendor, and how you sequence a process change for real subcontractors. Several inputs are deliberately incomplete, on inconsistent bases, or contain a quirk that a quick read would miss — that is normal for a live house file, and how you handle it is the point. Treat the DECISIONS log (Task 4) as ordinary purchasing hygiene: a buyer who can't say why they awarded a bid or held an invoice can't defend it to Construction, Sales, or CBUSA. Hard cap: ~2 hours. Prefer depth on the four tasks over extra polish; if you run short, leave a stub and note in your log what you would have done.
case.repoSeed:
A single-home working set for Plan 'Birchwood 2310', Lot 27, Maplewood Trace:
• House file — architectural plan set, the buyer Selection Sheet, and per-trade detailed Scopes; it also contains a previously approved field-change note (a footing/grade adjustment) buried two pages into the framing notes.
• Trim-Carpentry Bid Packet — three subcontractor proposals on mixed bases: Apex Trim & Door LLC (lump sum, excludes door hardware and closet shelving), Greenline Finish Carpentry (per-opening unit price + separate stair-parts line), and J. Ruiz Millwork (lump sum, includes hardware but is a non-CBUSA-covered vendor). Allowances and exclusions differ across all three.
• SpecWriter scope for the trim/finish-carpentry package (the 'common scope' the bids should map to).
• 'Options & Change Orders' Excel workbook — base allowances by category plus a pending request CO-118 from Sales: change great-room flooring from carpet to LVP and add a gas stub for a range.
• Vendor/subcontractor database extract — W-9 status, lead times, and CBUSA rebate / co-op-advertising flags per vendor.
• Invoice batch (5 vendor invoices) to match against the issued POs/WOs — includes one quantity overage, one unit-price mismatch versus the PO, and one invoice from a vendor with a missing W-9. One apparent overage is actually explained by the approved field change in the house file.
• Current 'PO/WO Process' document — partly paper: printed POs, emailed/faxed WOs, and hand-stamped invoice approval, with no 3-way match.
• CBUSA category list (covered vs non-CBUSA categories) and a one-page rebate / co-op-advertising program summary.
• Production slot schedule for Lot 27, including the buyer-selection cutoff date.
tasks: Level the three Trim-Carpentry proposals in the Bid Packet onto the common SpecWriter scope and recommend an award. Normalize the mixed bases (lump sum vs per-opening unit), add back each bidder's exclusions so the comparison is apples-to-apples, account for the non-CBUSA vendor and any CBUSA rebate/co-op eligibility and lead-time differences, and list the 2–3 clarifying questions you would send a bidder before you cut the PO/WO.

Price change order CO-118 from Sales (carpet→LVP in the great room + add a gas stub for a range) against the Birchwood house file, Selection Sheet, and the flooring/plumbing scopes. Price the delta versus the base allowances only, supplement the takeoff for the change, identify the cascading trade impacts (e.g., subfloor/transition, plumbing/gas rough), and state the production-slot and selection-cutoff coordination you would confirm with Construction before you quote Sales a number.

Run a 3-way match on the 5-invoice batch against the issued POs and WOs. Read the house file before disputing anything: clear the variances that are actually authorized, flag the genuine exceptions (over-billing, unit-price mismatch, compliance/W-9 gap), and note any material-utilization/waste signal. Then propose the single match rule (tolerance band + house-file/approval check) that would have caught the real issues automatically — this is the seed for the paperless invoice step.

Write a one-page recommendation to the management committee for advancing the PO/WO system toward paperless (including invoices), and keep a short DECISIONS log across all four tasks. In the log, for every open call you made — the bid-award basis, the CO-118 pricing scope, the invoice tolerance, and the paperless sequencing — record what you chose, the alternative you rejected, and the one question you would have asked Construction, Sales, or CBUSA.

coverProbes.where: Task 1 — the three Trim-Carpentry bids are quoted on different bases with different inclusions/exclusions, and the lowest headline number excludes scope the others carry.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate normalizes scope before comparing, adds back excluded hardware/shelving/stair parts, and weighs lead time, quality history, and CBUSA rebate eligibility against raw price; a naive one picks the lowest sticker number and issues the PO.
decisionSpace: Award to the lowest NORMALIZED total cost after adding back excluded scope — cost-first, but leans on a still-incomplete scope and may invite back-charges later.
Award the qualified/incumbent sub at a slightly higher normalized price for proven quality and reliable lead time — risk/quality-first, defensible but pays a premium.
Re-issue a single clarified scope sheet and re-bid before awarding — process-first, gets a clean comparison but spends time against the production slot.

coverProbes.where: Task 2 — pricing CO-118; a flat markup on the flooring line yields a clean, plausible number that passes a shallow check but misses cascading trades and the selection-cutoff/slot timing.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate checks what is already in the base allowance, prices only the true delta, surfaces the gas-stub plumbing rough and subfloor/transition cascade, and ties it to the production slot; a naive one marks up the line item and quotes Sales a number that under- or over-recovers and ignores schedule risk.
decisionSpace: Price the direct delta versus base allowance only and flag schedule risk separately — clean and defensible, but may under-recover the cascading work.
Price the delta plus cascading trades and an expedite/schedule adder because it is past the selection cutoff — full-cost recovery, higher quote that Sales may push back on.
Hold the change pending Construction's confirmation of slot impact before quoting — protects the build and the number, but slows Sales and the buyer.

coverProbes.where: Task 3 — one invoice 'overage' is actually explained by the approved field-change note buried in the framing notes of the house file.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate reads the house file and reconciles against documented approvals before disputing, so they clear the authorized variance and dispute only the real ones; a naive one auto-flags every line over tolerance and creates a false dispute that burns sub goodwill.
decisionSpace: Dispute every variance over tolerance uniformly — consistent and fast, but generates false positives and subcontractor friction.
Reconcile each variance against house-file approvals first, dispute only unauthorized ones — accurate, but more manual and slower at volume.
Set a $/% tolerance band that auto-approves small variances and disputes above it — scalable for the paperless goal, but lets minor leakage and waste pass unexamined.

coverProbes.where: Task 4 — 'advance the PO/WO system toward paperless, including invoices' is left open on scope, sequencing, and how low-tech subcontractors adopt it.
coverProbes.reveals: A strong candidate scopes the rollout, decides what gets the 3-way match first, plans for subs without email/portals, and names what stays manual; a naive one answers 'buy software' with no sequencing or adoption plan.
decisionSpace: Incremental — digitize POs/WOs first, layer invoice 3-way match later — low risk, but the AP/waste payoff arrives slowly.
Platform-first — adopt/extend the ERP/SpecWriter module end-to-end — fastest integration, but carries cost and subcontractor change-management risk.
Hybrid — standardize templates and e-approval now, defer a full sub portal until adoption is proven — pragmatic, but some paper/manual steps persist.
